paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent may need to pursue several competing objectives, with their relative importance changing between tasks. A policy that works well for one set of priorities can perform poorly under another. This paper studies how to learn a single model that supports different priorities and can adapt when those priorities are initially unknown.

The approach assumes linear preferences: the objectives are combined according to preference weights. The authors generalize the Bellman equation, which relates decisions to their future returns, so that one parametric representation can describe optimal policies across the preference space. This makes preferences part of the learning problem instead of fixing one reward combination in advance.

After initial training, the agent can execute the optimal policy for a supplied preference or infer an underlying preference from very few samples. Experiments in four domains demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The contribution connects learning across multiple objectives with rapid adaptation, within the stated setting of linear preferences.
neurips-2019-a-generalized-algorithm-for.tldr: A generalized Bellman equation lets one model learn policies across linear objective preferences and adapt from very few samples.

paragraphs: Optimization with noisy gradients has two related challenges: making rapid initial progress and continuing to improve once gradient noise becomes the dominant obstacle. This paper develops a general acceleration framework for convex and strongly convex objectives. Its aim is to improve suitable existing optimization methods through reusable mechanisms.

The framework extends Catalyst, an acceleration approach originally developed for deterministic objectives, to stochastic optimization. It starts with a method that has mild convergence guarantees on strongly convex problems. The analysis addresses both accelerated progress toward the region dominated by noise and subsequent convergence with optimal worst-case complexity depending on gradient noise variance.

The paper also provides a general analysis of inexact proximal operators, optimization steps that may themselves be difficult to compute precisely. This helps explain how stochastic methods behave when those steps are only approximated. Together, these contributions address acceleration and robustness to imperfect computation within the stated convex setting, while explicitly accounting for noise in the available gradients.
neurips-2019-a-generic-acceleration-fram.tldr: The framework extends Catalyst to accelerate stochastic convex optimization while accounting for gradient noise and approximate proximal steps.

paragraphs: Learning a value function means estimating the future return associated with states or actions. Many reinforcement learning methods update these estimates through Bellman fixed-point iterations rather than by minimizing an explicit objective. When the relevant update operator is not a contraction, those iterations can lose their convergence guarantees and may diverge.

This paper introduces a kernel loss for solving the Bellman equation using standard gradient-based optimization with convergence guarantees. A central advantage is that its gradient can be approximated from sampled transitions. It avoids the requirement for double samples that complicates earlier approaches such as residual gradient methods, making the objective more convenient to optimize from experience.

The approach accommodates general function classes, including neural networks, and can use either on-policy or off-policy data. Experiments report reliable and effective behavior across several benchmarks, including classic examples where standard algorithms diverge. The contribution brings an explicit optimization objective and practical gradient estimation to a learning problem where unstable updates can otherwise obstruct progress.
neurips-2019-a-kernel-loss-for-solving-t.tldr: A kernel loss enables gradient-based value learning with convergence guarantees and avoids the double-sampling requirement of earlier residual methods.

paragraphs: Linear inverse problems involve recovering a signal from observations that have been transformed and corrupted by noise. A denoising autoencoder can supply a learned prior to guide this recovery. However, existing methods using such priors estimate the noise parameter empirically or leave it as a setting that must be tuned.

Autoencoder guided EM, or AGEM, jointly addresses signal recovery and noise estimation. It provides a Bayesian inference framework for deep priors whose probability calculations are intractable. The authors show how to obtain efficient posterior samples using Metropolis-Hastings, enabling a Monte Carlo version of expectation-maximization to work with the autoencoder prior.

The method produces competitive results on signal denoising, image deblurring, and image devignetting. Its significance is the integration of learned representations with uncertainty-aware statistical inference: the deep prior guides reconstruction while the inference procedure also estimates the noise parameter. The reported applications demonstrate this combination across several recovery tasks without requiring noise to remain an externally tuned hyperparameter.
neurips-2019-agem-solving-linear-inverse.tldr: AGEM combines denoising autoencoder priors with posterior sampling to reconstruct signals and estimate their noise parameter jointly.

paragraphs: Pretrained language models can serve as general-purpose sentence encoders, turning text into representations useful for other tasks. This paper asks whether they can also serve as general-purpose decoders. That possibility requires a continuous representation that causes the model to reproduce any particular target sentence of interest.

The authors deliberately separate this question from the harder task of building an encoder that reliably produces those representations. They introduce two complementary ways to feed representations into pretrained unconditional language models, together with methods for mapping sentences into and out of the resulting reparametrized sentence space. They then investigate when a point in that space can generate a desired sentence.

The study finds that arbitrary sentences can be recovered nearly perfectly using models and representations of moderate size. This supports the feasibility of using such models as decoders through continuous representations. The result concerns finding representations that enable recovery; designing a general encoder to produce them remains outside the problem the paper chooses to solve.
neurips-2019-can-unconditional-language-.tldr: The study finds continuous representations that let pretrained unconditional language models recover arbitrary sentences nearly perfectly.

paragraphs: Distributed training can spend substantial time synchronizing workers instead of computing updates. Local stochastic gradient descent reduces that communication by letting workers train independently between synchronization rounds. This paper studies the resulting trade-off: how much communication can be reduced while retaining useful convergence behavior.

The authors provide a non-asymptotic error analysis, describing behavior at finite amounts of computation. It supports comparisons with two endpoints: one-shot averaging, where independent workers communicate once, and mini-batch averaging, where they communicate at every step. The analysis therefore places periodic synchronization within a common framework for assessing these alternatives.

For step sizes decreasing as t to the power of negative alpha, with alpha between one-half and one, the paper gives adaptive lower bounds on communication frequency. It also establishes a communication reduction factor of O(sqrt(T)/P^(3/2)), where T is the total number of gradients and P is the number of machines. This expression makes the stated saving depend explicitly on both computation and worker count.
neurips-2019-communication-trade-offs-fo.tldr: A finite-computation analysis quantifies how Local-SGD can reduce synchronization under the studied large-step-size schedules.

paragraphs: When many experiments produce noisy results, the analyst wants to estimate the true effect behind each observation. Auxiliary information about the experiments can help, but it does not replace the experimental measurements. This paper develops a way to combine both sources rather than relying on either one alone.

The proposed plug-in empirical Bayes estimator is flexible enough to incorporate any black-box predictive model. This allows predictive information from covariates to contribute alongside the noisy outcomes within a shared estimation procedure. The central idea is to make the information sources work together when neither captures everything relevant to the underlying effects.

For a simple data-generating model, the authors show that the estimator performs within a constant factor of the minimax benchmark, the best worst-case estimation performance. They also establish robust convergence guarantees under considerably broader conditions. Results on real and simulated data are promising, supporting the practical value of combining these inputs while keeping the strongest optimality statement tied to the specified simple model.
neurips-2019-covariate-powered-empirical.tldr: A flexible empirical Bayes estimator combines noisy experimental outcomes with covariate predictions and provides theoretical and empirical support.

paragraphs: Finding vulnerable functions in source code helps developers identify where repairs are needed, but manual inspection is demanding and requires security expertise. Devign approaches this task through graph-level classification. It learns from rich graph representations of program semantics, drawing on the idea that code relationships can reveal vulnerability patterns.

The model uses a graph neural network to learn node representations and introduces a Conv module to extract useful features from them for classifying whole graphs. The training datasets are manually labeled and drawn from four diverse, large open-source C projects. This grounds the evaluation in complex real source code with varied behavior.

The reported evaluation shows average improvements over prior leading methods of 10.51% in accuracy and 8.68% in F1 score. The Conv module contributes average gains of 4.66% in accuracy and 6.37% in F1. These findings support both the overall use of learned program representations and the feature-extraction module's contribution on the evaluated datasets.
neurips-2019-devign-effective-vulnerabil.tldr: Devign learns graph representations of program semantics to identify vulnerable functions, improving reported performance on real C-project datasets.

paragraphs: Finding a particular image of a complex scene can require several descriptions, especially when the scene contains multiple objects. This paper studies an interactive search process in which a user supplies successive natural-language queries to refine the results. Each round adds information about the image the user wants.

Drill-down encodes those multiple queries in a compact state representation, extending methods designed for a single retrieval round. The representation lets the system use the accumulated descriptions during search. The authors also find that existing image datasets with captions provide effective weak supervision, making caption information useful for learning this interactive task.

The evaluation covers two proposed benchmarks: simulated retrieval using region captions as queries, and interactive retrieval with queries supplied by human evaluators. Drill-down outperforms the compared sequential encoding and embedding networks. The findings show that multiple language-query rounds can be effective for locating highly specific complex scenes, and that useful training signals can come from captioned images.
neurips-2019-drill-down-interactive-retr.tldr: Drill-down combines successive language queries in a compact representation to retrieve increasingly specific images of complex scenes.

paragraphs: Small changes to an input can cause a classifier to make a mistake. Existing theory connects this vulnerability to concentration: a property of a probability space in which any set containing a substantial share of probability lies close to almost every point. Under the relevant concentration condition, small adversarial perturbations are inevitable.

The practical question is whether actual image distributions have the concentration needed for those theoretical conclusions. This paper introduces a method for measuring and bounding concentration empirically on a concrete dataset. The authors prove that the method converges to the actual concentration, linking a measurable estimate to the underlying mathematical property.

They apply the method to several image classification benchmarks to estimate intrinsic robustness against L2 and L-infinity perturbations. These estimates investigate limits associated with the data distribution itself. The contribution makes a previously abstract explanation of adversarial vulnerability empirically examinable, while preserving the central condition: the theoretical inevitability result depends on inputs coming from a concentrated space.
neurips-2019-empirically-measuring-conce.tldr: A convergent empirical method measures data concentration to investigate distribution-dependent limits on image-classification robustness.

paragraphs: Exploration requires deciding not only what information to collect but also how to reach it efficiently. The paper argues that existing heuristic-driven strategies can waste many steps passing through states they already understand. This happens when their exploration heuristics fit the environment's dynamics poorly, even though the strategies have attractive theoretical properties.

The proposed Value Iteration for Exploration Cost algorithm, or VIEC, plans exploration explicitly. It solves an augmented Markov decision process to compute an optimal exploration scheme. This makes the cost of collecting the required data part of the planning problem, rather than relying entirely on a predefined exploration heuristic.

On some tower-shaped environments, the analysis shows popular strategies requiring O(n^2md) or O(n^2m + nmd) steps, while the optimal scheme obtained by VIEC requires O(nmd). Here n and m count states and actions, and d is the data demand. These examples establish concrete weaknesses of the analyzed strategies and illustrate the potential benefit of planning exploration explicitly.
neurips-2019-explicit-planning-for-effic.tldr: VIEC explicitly plans data collection and achieves better exploration-step scaling than analyzed heuristics on certain tower-shaped environments.

paragraphs: Least-mean-squares solvers support regression and serve as components in other learning methods. This paper accelerates such computation through a compact, exact summary of vectors. Given n vectors of dimension d, its algorithm returns a weighted subset of d+1 vectors whose weighted sum exactly matches the original sum.

A construction based on Caratheodory's theorem already provides such a subset, but its O(n^2d^2) runtime makes it impractical for this purpose. The new algorithm takes O(nd) time by making O(log n) calls to that construction on carefully selected small subsets. Its design combines two approaches to summarizing data: sketches and coresets.

As an application, the authors use these summaries to improve existing least-mean-squares solvers, including implementations in scikit-learn, reporting speedups of up to 100 times. They also describe straightforward extensions to streaming and distributed data. The exactness claim concerns the preserved vector sum, while the application results demonstrate how that mathematical summary can support faster solver computation.
neurips-2019-fast-and-accurate-least-mea.tldr: An exact vector-summarization algorithm runs in O(nd) time and supports reported least-mean-squares solver speedups of up to 100 times.

paragraphs: A generative adversarial network should learn patterns that extend beyond its training examples. This paper examines that generalization problem through privacy protection, connecting dependence on training data with the risk of overfitting. The perspective also motivates measuring how much information a trained GAN exposes about its training set.

The theoretical result shows that using a differentially private learning algorithm to train a GAN bounds its generalization gap. This provides a qualified control on overfitting rather than a claim that overfitting disappears. The same privacy-based insight offers a way to reinterpret existing approaches, including Bayesian GANs.

To investigate leakage quantitatively, the authors perform membership attacks on trained models, testing whether training-set membership can be inferred. They find that existing Lipschitz regularization techniques both reduce the generalization gap and alleviate information leakage. The paper therefore combines a theoretical privacy-to-generalization connection with empirical evidence that a regularization approach can help on both fronts, without claiming that the measured leakage is eliminated.
neurips-2019-generalization-in-generativ.tldr: The paper links private GAN training to bounded generalization gaps and finds that Lipschitz regularization also reduces measured information leakage.

paragraphs: Graph-based semi-supervised learning often treats connected nodes as likely to share a label. That assumption can be unreliable when edges are noisy or represent relationships unrelated to labels. Graph Agreement Models address this mismatch by learning which pairs should be encouraged to receive matching predictions.

An auxiliary agreement model uses node features to predict the probability that two nodes have the same label. During classifier training, agreement is encouraged only for pairs judged likely to match. The agreement model and node classifier are trained jointly through co-training, allowing the learned agreement signal to guide the classifier toward better local optima.

The method can augment graph convolutional networks and neural graph learning approaches. It can also induce a graph for semi-supervised classification when none is supplied. Experiments report relative improvements of up to 72% for various node classifiers and state-of-the-art results on multiple established datasets. These findings support replacing an indiscriminate neighborhood-agreement assumption with a learned, feature-dependent assessment.
neurips-2019-graph-agreement-models-for-.tldr: Graph Agreement Models learn which node pairs likely share labels and use that signal to improve semi-supervised classification.

paragraphs: Estimating an optimal transport map becomes difficult in high dimensions. One existing approach breaks the problem into successive one-dimensional transport problems along random projection directions. The paper identifies a weakness of that strategy: randomly chosen directions can lead to slow convergence or failure to converge in practice.

Projection pursuit Monge map, or PPMM, selects projection directions adaptively. It combines projection pursuit regression with sufficient dimension reduction to identify the most informative direction at each iteration. The authors theoretically show that the dimension-reduction procedure consistently estimates that direction, giving the selection rule a statistical justification.

The paper also establishes weak convergence of PPMM to the target transport map in a reasonable number of steps. Empirical results describe the procedure as computationally easy and fast to converge, with finite-sample evaluations involving Wasserstein distance estimation and generative models. Its central contribution is a principled way to choose useful one-dimensional problems, supported by both convergence analysis and application results.
neurips-2019-large-scale-optimal-transpo.tldr: PPMM adaptively chooses informative projection directions to estimate large-scale optimal transport maps, with theoretical and empirical convergence support.

paragraphs: Deep-network optimization exhibits behaviors that can be difficult to reconcile within a single picture of the loss landscape. This paper proposes a phenomenological model: a geometric description intended to organize observed behavior. High dimensionality is central, with interconnected high-dimensional wedges forming a large-scale structure that attracts optimization.

The authors experimentally examine how learning rate, network width, and L2 regularization affect the optimizer's path. They find that these choices influence the large-scale curvature of explored regions in similar ways. The proposed geometry therefore connects several apparently different training choices through their effects on where optimization travels.

The model also leads to predictions about connections among trained solutions. The paper demonstrates low-loss subspaces connecting a set of solutions, extending the idea of connections between only two solutions. It additionally interprets deep-network ensembling techniques through the same geometric perspective. The contribution is an experimentally supported organizing model that relates optimization paths, connected solutions, and ensembling within one account.
neurips-2019-large-scale-structure-of-ne.tldr: An experimentally supported wedge-based model connects hyperparameter effects, optimization paths, and low-loss subspaces joining multiple neural-network solutions.

paragraphs: Options learned in a simulator must cope with uncertainty in that simulator's parameters. Optimizing only average performance can leave poor outcomes insufficiently addressed, while optimizing only the worst case can weaken ordinary performance. This paper seeks options that work well across both average and unfavorable cases.

The proposed method uses conditional value at risk, or CVaR, to account for adverse outcomes during learning. The authors extend an existing CVaR policy-gradient method to robust Markov decision processes and apply the extension to learning options. This provides a way to address model uncertainty while considering more than just one extreme of the performance distribution.

Experiments use the multi-joint robot control tasks HopperIceBlock, Half-Cheetah, and Walker2D. The resulting options achieve better worst-case performance than options trained only to minimize average loss, and better average performance than options trained only to minimize worst-case loss. These comparisons demonstrate the intended balance on the evaluated tasks; they do not assert superiority over each comparison method on both criteria.
neurips-2019-learning-robust-options-by-.tldr: CVaR-based option learning improves worst-case performance over average-only training and average performance over worst-case-only training in robot-control experiments.

paragraphs: Repeatedly evaluating models on the same test set raises concerns about overfitting to that benchmark. Yet replication studies suggest that some heavily reused benchmarks still track meaningful progress. This paper offers an explanation based on prediction similarity: many of the models being compared behave alike on individual examples.

The authors show empirically that models submitted to the ImageNet ILSVRC benchmark agree more than their accuracy levels alone would imply. They also observe substantial similarity among models produced by large-scale hyperparameter search. These findings make agreement between predictions relevant to understanding the consequences of repeated evaluation.

Motivated by those observations, the paper proves a non-asymptotic generalization bound that explicitly incorporates model similarity. The bound yields meaningful confidence statements in practical settings and establishes that similarity can mitigate overfitting from test-set reuse. The result supplies a qualified explanation for benchmark longevity: the effects of reuse depend in part on how similar the evaluated models are, rather than solely on how often evaluation occurs.
neurips-2019-model-similarity-mitigates-.tldr: Prediction similarity helps explain benchmark longevity and enables generalization bounds that account for repeated test-set use.

paragraphs: Seeded segmentation and graph-based semi-supervised learning assign unlabeled nodes to supplied seeds or labels. The usual Watershed approach does this through a minimum spanning forest connecting every node to a seed. This paper considers all possible spanning forests and asks how likely each seed-to-node connection is under forest sampling.

The resulting Probabilistic Watershed gives a probability for a node to connect to a particular seed. Its equivalence to Random Walker methods and harmonic energy minimization was already known. The authors provide a simpler proof and use Kirchhoff's matrix tree theorem to establish that computing the probabilistic approach is feasible.

The paper also establishes a new connection between Random Walker probabilities and the triangle inequality for effective resistance. Finally, it derives an intuitive interpretation of Power Watershed. These contributions bring several graph-labeling methods into a common mathematical picture, explaining probabilistic assignments through spanning forests and clarifying relationships among approaches that initially appear to use different constructions.
neurips-2019-probabilistic-watershed-sam.tldr: Probabilistic Watershed interprets graph labeling through all spanning forests and clarifies connections to Random Walker and Power Watershed methods.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning algorithms often change their exploration policy as new data arrive. Frequent adaptation can be difficult to implement in real applications. This paper studies how an agent can keep learning effectively while changing its policy infrequently, using local switching cost to quantify that aspect of adaptivity.

The main algorithm combines model-free Q-learning with UCB2 exploration in episodic Markov decision processes of H steps. Over K episodes, it achieves sublinear regret with local switching cost O(H^3SA log K), where S and A count states and actions. Sublinear regret means that the cumulative performance shortfall grows more slowly than the number of episodes.

The authors also prove a lower bound of Omega(HSA) on local switching cost for any no-regret algorithm, showing that some switching is unavoidable in this setting. They adapt their algorithm to concurrent learning, obtaining improvements over prior work in certain aspects. Together, the results make policy-change frequency an explicit theoretical consideration alongside learning performance.
neurips-2019-provably-efficient-q-learni.tldr: Q-learning with UCB2 achieves sublinear regret with bounded local switching cost, while a lower bound shows some switching is unavoidable.

paragraphs: Storing several learned models usually raises the question of how much parameter storage each requires. This paper presents a method in which multiple models coexist within a single set of parameters. The models remain individually retrievable, so the shared parameter instance can hold several distinguishable learned models.

The experiments investigate both storage and continued learning. They show that a surprisingly large number of neural-network models can be stored effectively in one parameter instance. Each model can also undergo thousands of training steps without significantly interfering with the others in the superposition. This matters because the shared storage remains useful while individual models continue to change.

The authors frame the approach as an online complement to compression. Conventional compression reduces a network's size after training, whereas superposition uses otherwise unrealized capacity during training. The reported results support the possibility of storing and updating multiple models together with limited interference. The claim is empirical and qualified by effective retrieval and the observed degree of interference.
neurips-2019-superposition-of-many-model.tldr: Multiple neural-network models can share one parameter set while remaining retrievable and tolerating thousands of training steps with little observed interference.

paragraphs: How much data is needed to recover the parameters of a convolutional network? This paper studies that question for networks with one hidden layer and non-overlapping filters. It proposes approximate gradient descent and analyzes both the speed of parameter recovery and the number of samples required.

Starting from random initialization, the algorithm converges linearly to the ground-truth parameters up to statistical precision, with high probability. The result covers general nontrivial activation functions that are monotonic and Lipschitz continuous, including ReLU, Leaky ReLU, Sigmoid, and Softplus. This broadens the activation functions covered by the analysis while retaining the specified network structure.

The sample requirement improves on earlier results in its dependence on hidden-node count and filter size. It also matches an information-theoretic lower bound for the linear-activation case, suggesting tight sample complexity. Numerical experiments support the theory. The lower-bound comparison is specifically to linear activations, so its broader significance is evidence of tightness rather than a separately established lower bound for every covered activation.
neurips-2019-tight-sample-complexity-of-.tldr: Approximate gradient descent learns the studied one-hidden-layer CNNs with improved sample complexity and high-probability linear convergence up to statistical precision.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search can discover strong network designs, but many systems are built around particular applications. General hyperparameter-optimization tools offer broader coverage while lacking convenient constructs for describing architecture choices. This paper addresses that gap with a formal language for search spaces over general computational graphs.

The language supports modular, composable, reusable descriptions of candidate architectures. It also separates the implementation of a search space from the algorithm that explores it. A consistent interface exposes the same space to different search algorithms, making the description of possible architectures an independent component that can be reused.

The authors encode search spaces from the architecture-search literature and demonstrate experiments combining different spaces and search algorithms. These combinations can be explored without implementing every pairing from scratch. The contribution is a programming foundation for architecture search: it makes search-space design easier to express and reason about while reducing repeated implementation work. The paper also releases an implementation of the language.
neurips-2019-towards-modular-and-program.tldr: A formal language makes architecture-search spaces modular and reusable through a consistent interface to different search algorithms.

paragraphs: Attention over graph nodes is intended to help a graph neural network focus on useful information. This paper asks when that mechanism actually improves performance, especially when models encounter larger, more complex, or noisier graphs. The authors create simple graph-reasoning tasks to study these effects under controlled conditions.

The results show that attention is often negligible or even harmful under typical conditions. Under certain conditions, however, it produces gains exceeding 60% on some classification tasks. Achieving those favorable conditions in practice is challenging and often requires optimal initialization or direct supervision of the attention mechanism. The benefit therefore depends strongly on how attention is learned.

The authors propose weakly supervised attention training as an alternative. It approaches the performance of supervised models and improves on unsupervised models across several synthetic and real datasets. The study provides both a diagnostic account of attention's uneven effectiveness and a training approach that helps realize its benefits without relying on the fully supervised setup.
neurips-2019-understanding-attention-and.tldr: Controlled graph tasks reveal conditional benefits from attention, and weak supervision helps approach the performance of supervised attention.

paragraphs: Community detection describes a graph's broader group structure, while node representation learning captures information about individual nodes and local structure. These tasks are often studied separately despite their close relationship. vGraph combines them in a probabilistic generative model so that community membership and node representations are learned collaboratively.

The model assumes each node is a mixture of communities and each community is a multinomial distribution over nodes. Low-dimensional representations of nodes and communities parameterize both the mixture coefficients and community distributions. A variational inference algorithm trains the model through backpropagation while encouraging neighboring nodes to have similar community memberships in the latent space.

Experiments on multiple real-world graphs show strong performance on both tasks, exceeding many competitive baselines. The framework can also be extended to identify hierarchical communities. The contribution is a shared probabilistic account of group membership and node representation, supported by results on both outputs rather than treating one solely as a preliminary step for the other.
neurips-2019-vgraph-a-generative-model-f.tldr: vGraph jointly learns community memberships and node representations through a generative mixture model, improving both tasks on evaluated real-world graphs.
